title: Calculated Risk: Checking the Evidence and the Cost
header_line: My analysis of one book on an entrepreneur's life. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: Do you take risks, or do you calculate them?
A calculated risk is a risk taken after checking the evidence for how it can be reduced, even when it looks like an all-in bet from outside.
A student said: the person in the book does not value money. He would sleep under an overpass to be in a space where he puts all his money on the line.
He realizes he needs money, but he doesn't let money be a distraction to the mission. He understands it is a consequence of the mission.

Let's pay attention to the evidence of how the person in the book mitigates risk. It comes across as: I'll risk everything, like the poker game where he kept doubling until he won and then walked away with the money. But I think he is very calculated in his risk.
The book's idea: the idiot index compares how much a finished product costs with the cost of its basic materials.
A student found the evidence in how the person in the book thinks about cost against the overall cost of everything. The passage from the book follows.
which calculated how much more costly a finished product was than the cost of the basic materials.

So he is mitigating risk. He is not just going and buying a rocket that is overpriced. He asks what the components are, and what the carbon fibre, the metal and the fuel cost. I'm not going to believe anything at face value.
A student said: another lesson: after his risk assessment and the cost of everything, he concluded they could do it themselves. They just needed the information, the data and the qualified people.
Before you take or price a risk, find the cost of the basic parts and the gap to the price. That is how a bold bet becomes a calculated one.
Next idea: price set against cost. The next lesson, "Price against cost", applies the same test to show where a price is speculation.
What is the real cost of the thing you buy or sell?

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write the price of something you buy often.
Write what its basic parts cost.
Write the gap between them, as a multiple.
Write the risk you take that is calculated and the risk that is only nerve.
Write what you could build yourself if you gathered the data and the people.

check.q: A founder says they will risk everything on a plan. What shows the risk is still calculated, in the lesson's terms?
choices: The founder asks other people to approve each step of the plan first
The founder checks the evidence on how to reduce the risk
The founder spends a long time planning every detail in advance
The founder keeps the plan secret until it is nearly finished

check.q: A product sells for much more than the cost of its basic materials. What does the idiot index show?
choices: The gap between the finished price and the cost of its materials
The profit the seller has set for the product over the year
The number of other firms that sell the same kind of product
The cost of the labour used to make and ship the product

check.q: Why does the lesson say money did not distract the person from the mission?
choices: Money was never needed for the mission to go ahead
Money was left to other people to look after for the person
Money was treated as a consequence of the mission
Money was kept apart from the mission in a separate fund

recap: A bold bet becomes a calculated one when you check the evidence. The idiot index compares a finished price with the cost of its basic materials.
